newsitem.title: UK: Euro bourses buoyant but edgy over Dow.
newsitem.headline: Euro bourses buoyant but edgy over Dow.

text.p: Leading European stock markets took heart from Wall Street's third consecutive overnight surge to move modestly higher on Thursday.
On the currency front, the dollar remained weaker against the yen amid growing concerns about the burgeoning U.S. trade deficit with Japan.
London, Frankfurt and Paris blue chips rose in step at their open, but uncertainty whether the rally in the Dow Jones Industrial Average was sustainable helped to dampen morning European gains.
"People are getting twitchy about the Dow," said one London-based trader.

German shares turned in the morning's strongest performance, with the DAX index of floor trading up nearly one percent. A weaker-than-expected March business sentiment report and absence of underlying inflationary concerns underpinned the market.
Engineering giant Daimler Benz shed nearly 4.5 marks after analysts expressed disappointment at a meeting with management following the company results' announcement on Wednesday.
London shares shook off some of their morning reserve, climbing nearly 10 points by late morning.
Although Britain reported slightly lower-than-expected March inflation, the positive news failed to ignite the market.
Fears over near-term U.S. and UK interest rate rises, continuing pressure from a strong pound and worries over post-election changes to corporate taxes were all weighing on sentiment, traders said.
"We are now two weeks away from an election and the volatility is concerning people," one said. "People do not want this market to run away with itself. That is why we haven't reflected Wall Street."

French stocks slipped back after gaining nearly half a percent at the open. Carmaker Peugeot weighed on the market, pulling the auto sector lower, after it posted a disappointing 57 percent drop and announced a dividend cut.
In currencies, the dollar suffered as Japan's March overall trade surplus fell sharply but posted an 11.2 percent rise with the United States, heightening trade tension between the two countries.
Japanese authorities appear eager to let some steam out of the dollar's rally but would be happy to see a gentle landing that keeps the U.S. currency on a firm trend against the yen, analysts said.

Japanese intervention was on the cards, they added, especially after recent strong messages from Japanese officials about the yen's fall and Washington's growing worries over the renewed rise in Japan's trade surplus.
U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers warned overnight of trade friction unless Japan became less reliant on exports and promoted growth from within.
All eyes were firmly focused on U.S. trade data (due at 1230 gmt), particularly the U.S.-Japan gap, which many expected to widen further.
Senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara also said there was growing political pressure for Japan to raise its official discount rate, which gave support to the yen.

"As time progresses and the economy looks like coming out of recession, this pressure to raise rates will increase and will go a long way to take the pressure off dollar/yen," said Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull's Davies.
CURRENCIES AT 1100 GMT
The dollar was quoted at 1.7279 marks and 125.81 yen after ending at 1.7285 and 125.80 in late trading in Europe on Wednesday.
STOCK MARKETS AT 1100 GMT
LONDON - The FTSE-100 index was up 9.4 points at 4,304.0.
PARIS - The CAC-40 was up 2.35 points at 2,623.32.
FRANKFURT - The 30-share DAX index was up 32.16 points at 3,385.61.
PRECIOUS METALS
Gold was fixed in London at $341.20 versus $339.65 at the close in London on Wednesday. Silver was four cents higher at $4.84.
